analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal and state energy-efficiency standards for appliances and equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have wiped out federal and state appliance efficiency standards, died in committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Department of Energy's authority to set energy and water efficiency standards for consumer and commercial products, erased every existing federal standard, and barred states from having their own, nullifying the ones already on the books. Those standards require appliances like refrigerators, furnaces, and air conditioners to meet minimum efficiency levels, which lowers utility bills for the people who use them. Without them, manufacturers could sell less efficient products, and households would pay more on their energy bills for decades. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of appliances, heating and cooling equipment, and industrial machinery would gain if the bill passed, because they would no longer have to meet federal efficiency or testing requirements and could sell cheaper-to-make, less efficient models. Retailers selling those products would face no efficiency rules either.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Department of Energy's authority to set energy and water conservation standards for consumer and commercial products and repeals all existing standards [S2].
Prohibits any state or federal agency from adopting or keeping an energy conservation or water efficiency requirement for a product, nullifying existing state standards [S2] [S3].
Repeals the federal standards program for certain industrial equipment, replacing federal test procedures with 'generally accepted industry testing procedures' chosen by industry [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses would pay through higher electricity, natural gas, and water bills, because appliances and equipment sold after repeal would use more energy over their lifetimes than the standards currently require. States would also lose standards they had adopted to protect their own residents.

drawbacks.text: Efficiency standards impose real compliance and testing costs on manufacturers, and the bill's 'free market' argument is that consumers should be free to buy cheaper, less efficient products if they prefer a lower purchase price [S3].
Some standards can raise the upfront purchase price of an appliance even as they lower monthly bills, which weighs heaviest on lower-income buyers who cannot afford the more efficient model.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to manufacturers from dropping efficiency rules would be small next to the added costs to the public: efficiency standards are one of the few policies that lower nearly every household's utility bills automatically, without anyone having to research or choose. Wiping out both federal and state standards at once, with no replacement, would lock in higher energy use and higher bills for the life of every appliance sold. The honest case for the bill rests on consumer choice and manufacturer costs, and it does not come close to balancing the ledger for energy users.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy Subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
On January 25, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary energy consumers came out ahead: because the bill died, existing federal and state efficiency standards stayed in force, keeping utility bills lower than they would have been under repeal. Manufacturers hoping to sell less efficient products without compliance costs did not get that change.

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal federal and state energy efficiency standards; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a member of the sponsor's own party
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote; the bill was sent to its Energy Subcommittee and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else signed on, so the bill's support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: Repeal would free them from federal efficiency and testing requirements and let them sell cheaper-to-make, less efficient models. Their savings would come out of household utility bills, since consumers would pay more to run each product for its lifetime [S2] [S3].

The bill repeals the federal standards program for certain industrial equipment outright and replaces federal test procedures with industry-chosen ones [S3]. Businesses buying that equipment would face higher operating energy costs.
Less efficient appliances and equipment mean more electricity and gas sold per household. Utilities would gain sales that show up as higher bills for their customers.
